opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jason Hansen (employee ID E044) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E044.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Jason Hansen (E044) is a full-time Engineer requesting admin access to Payroll. Full-time employees can be granted up to write; admin requires that the employee's role owns the system, and Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role. Requested access exceeds the allowed level, so recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jason Hansen (E044) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds the max, so recommend granting read for Payroll.
reason: Jason Hansen (E044) requests admin access to Payroll, which is owned by the Payroll Specialist role. Admin is never allowed here: full-time employees may have admin only if their role owns the system (E044 is an Engineer), and contractors are never granted admin. The two notes conflict on employment type (HR note: full_time → max write; Security note: contractor with basic training → max read, since write requires advanced training). Read is at or below the maximum under either interpretation, so it is the safe, policy-compliant grant since the requested admin exceeds the maximum.

2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role.

Jason is an Engineer (per note 1) or contractor (per note 2). Either way, his role doesn't own Payroll. So admin is not allowed.

If full-time: max write. If contractor with basic training: max read.
